When does a colony stop being a colony for UN purposes? Resolution 1541, adopted by the General Assembly in 1960, lays down the guiding tests. Under Article 73 of the Charter, states that rule overseas lands must send facts about them to the UN. A team of six had spent a year working out when that duty ends, building on a list of tests from 1953.

The Assembly thanks the team and approves its tests, with a few changes. Those tests weigh whether a land has gained full self-rule, joined a free state as an equal, or linked itself to one by free choice. The list became the yardstick of the great wave of decolonization that swept the 1960s.
un-ga-res-41:
First principles for cutting world armaments were set down in Resolution 41 of the General Assembly, passed on 14 December 1946. Under Article 11 of the Charter, the Assembly claims its part in guarding peace. It states the need for a swift, general ordering and cut of arms and armed forces, across all states at once.

The Security Council is urged to draft the workable steps at speed, in the order of their weight. The plans would go to member states for debate at a special session of the Assembly. Pacts approved there would then go to states for ratification under Article 26. Arms given up by all at once, never by a few alone, is the rule at the heart of the text.

All the peoples of the world, the first disarmament session held in 1978, hold a vital stake in the success of arms talks. All states have the right to sit in them. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d41: On October 14, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, in a message that became Document 41 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d141: On November 18, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, as the British party also closed on Cairo. His message is Document 141 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d241:
Patrick Hurley, the President's personal representative, wrote to Roosevelt from Cairo on 20 November 1943 after inspecting the China theater of operations. He had met Generals Stilwell and Chennault, toured with air commander Stratemeyer, and spent some six hours in talks with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek.

Hurley's conclusions are warm. Chiang trusts Roosevelt fully, favors democracy and liberty, opposes imperialism and communism. He will follow Roosevelt's lead on political questions at the coming conference. He hopes it restates the Atlantic Charter and the Four Freedoms. On strategy he holds one firm line: in the China theater he must remain supreme. He will not take a subordinate place under Lord Mountbatten. Still, he praises Mountbatten and offers full cooperation in Burma.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d341:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy sent Harry Hopkins a second memorandum at Cairo on 30 November 1943, separate from the civil affairs agreement of the same day. This one concerns a proposed joint committee for all French questions, an idea from Secretary Hull.

In his talk with Eden, McCloy had raised Hull's suggestion of a new body. It would be modeled somewhat on the combined committees. All dealings with the French would be cleared through it for the time being. Hull hoped it would end the irritation and distrust bred by the two nations' separate French policies. Eden approved promptly, and Hull cabled that the group should sit in London. McCloy pictures it as informal, a military man and a foreign affairs man from each government, drawing on other agencies as needed, and asks whether the President favors pushing it along.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d441: Under the number 441, the Cairo-Tehran volume prints a short editorial note. Department historians added notes like this one throughout the conference record. Their job is to fill gaps, give context, and flag related documents. The surrounding papers come from the Cairo and Tehran meetings of 1943. At those meetings the Allied leaders set the course for the war's next year. Treat the note as the editors speaking directly to the reader.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d541:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on January 7, 1944, in the opening week of the year the Tehran Conference had planned for. Churchill had recovered from the illness that struck him after Cairo. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The Roosevelt-Churchill correspondence never rested for long, and early January found the two governments converting summit decisions into the Normandy invasion plan. A Churchill letter of this date belongs to that conversion: priorities argued, resources counted, and two leaders keeping their partnership warm by constant writing. Readers see the alliance's engine room at the start of its biggest year.
frus-1944-quebec-d41:
Another Churchill message reached Roosevelt on August 31, 1944. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. It sits beside the day's other letter.

Two messages on the month's last day fit a pattern. A leader was clearing his desk before a voyage. The Quebec agenda was heavy that September. It covered the final campaigns in Europe. It covered Germany's treatment after defeat. It also covered the terms of American aid. For readers, the message shows Churchill arriving at the conference on paper. His British positions were argued in advance. The conference opened at Quebec City that September.
frus-1944-quebec-d141:
British chiefs of staff representatives answered the American strategy paper on September 2, 1944, in C.C.S. 654/1. They proposed three amendments to the basic undertakings Washington had drafted for the coming staff conference. In all other respects, they said, the American proposals were acceptable, which makes the small wording changes the real subject here.

One amendment added coordinated action with Russian forces to the pledge of aid, noting the armies were converging. Another extended assistance beyond French and Italian forces to other co-belligerents, such as Turkey or satellites changing sides. The third softened the rush to the Pacific: moving forces east should have regard to other inescapable commitments.
frus-1944-quebec-d241:
General Wilson asked the Combined Chiefs for guidance on economic policy for Italy on September 13, 1944. As the battle line moved north, he wrote, the operational phase was ending across large areas, and the approach to civilian supply and rehabilitation had to be re-examined. His directives, built for active operations, no longer fitted the situation he faced as president of the Control Commission.

The armistice promised Italians no material assistance, Wilson noted, yet an expectation of relief had arisen from both governments' known humanitarian policies. Governing only by military necessity risked losing a reasonably prosperous, contented postwar Italy. He cited a winter clothing program: he was now asked to certify it as the bare minimum to prevent disease and unrest, though it had been designed on estimated essential needs.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d41: Wilson Brown, the president's naval aide, wrote on 3 January 1945 to Admiral Charles Cooke, chief of staff to the fleet commander. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d141:
Had Roosevelt secretly agreed to the Curzon Line at Tehran? Harriman's memorandum of 16 October 1944 answers a Polish claim that he had. Polish Foreign Minister Romer called at Spaso House in Moscow with a letter from Premier Mikolajczyk. The paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Romer's letter concerned Molotov's account of the President's Tehran position. Harriman told him the account was wrong. Roosevelt had not agreed to the Curzon Line at Tehran. He had made plain he would take no stand on the boundary, in private or in public. Harriman also explained why he had not challenged Molotov at the meeting itself. He had sat there as an observer, and it was not the place to argue over what the President had said.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d241:
Iran gets a four-part treatment in this briefing paper of 6 January 1945, “Memoranda Concerning Iran.” Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary calls Iran a testing ground for three-power cooperation and for the principles of Dumbarton Oaks.

American policy backs Iranian independence and seeks to strengthen the country from within, so excuses for outside meddling shrink. michelet-proces-des-templiers-vol-1-1841:

michelet-proces-des-templiers-vol-2-1841:

quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol1-1841:
Jules Quicherat opened his great edition of Joan of Arc's trials in 1841 with the record of her condemnation. Procès de Condamnation et de Réhabilitation de Jeanne d'Arc, volume one, prints the Latin trial text of 1431. Joan was nineteen when a church court at Rouen sent her to the fire.

The volume gives the charges, the long questioning, and her answers as the court clerks wrote them down. Readers meet her voice under pressure, session by session. Quicherat's edition became the base for all later study of Joan. The first volume is where that study starts: in the courtroom itself.
robert-boron-saint-graal-michel-1841:
Robert de Boron gave the Grail its Christian root in two romances of the years around 1200. Le Roman du Saint-Graal, in Francisque Michel's 1841 edition of the Old French, holds his Joseph of Arimathea and his Merlin. No earlier texts bind the Grail cup to the Passion.

Joseph tells how the cup that held Christ's blood came west and who kept it. Merlin tells of the prophet's birth, his gifts, and his hand in Arthur's rise. Every later Grail tale, from the great cycles to Malory, descends from these two. Michel's edition prints the founding texts in their first tongue.
hawthorne-grandfathers-chair-1841:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Whole History of Grandfather's Chair in 1841, a history for children. The book tells New England history, from the Puritans to the Revolution, through one old chair. Hawthorne wrote it for young readers in the days before his fame as a romancer grew.

Grandfather, in a Boston parlor, traces his chair's owners through persecutions, wars, and witch trial years. The chair hears of Endicott, King Philip's War, and the Boston Tea Party in its long life. Children Laurence, Clara, and little Alice question, doubt, and dream over the tales by the fireside. Hawthorne makes dry annals into scenes a child can feel, without hiding the era's harsh deeds. It was a pioneer work of American history written for the young at home.
emerson-essays-first-series-1841:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Essays: First Series in 1841, with Self-Reliance and The Over-Soul inside. The book is the founding document of American intellectual independence in prose of rare force and fire. Emerson had honed the essays as lectures, and their voice still sounds spoken and urgent on the page.

Self-Reliance commands trust in one's own thought against conformity, consistency, and the crowd's dull pressure in life. The Over-Soul traces one spirit through all souls, the ground of his calm moral optimism in man. History, Compensation, and Circles round out a set that young America took as a charter of selfhood. carlyle-heroes-1841:

He treats the hero in six forms: god, prophet, poet, priest, man of letters, and king. Odin, Muhammad, Dante, Shakespeare, Luther, and Napoleon appear among them.

History, in his famous claim, is the biography of great men. The book stated the great-man theory in its classic form. It shaped Victorian biography and popular history for decades. Modern readers often resist its claims yet enjoy its force. It is a key text for the study of leadership myths.
cooper-deerslayer-1841:

Young Natty, called Deerslayer, joins his friend Chingachgook to rescue a kidnapped Delaware maiden from the Hurons. Around a floating ark and a settler's lake castle, scalp hunters and soldiers push Natty toward his first killing. He takes a human life reluctantly and earns a new name, Hawkeye. Cooper builds the moral code of the American hero here: merciful, truthful, and deadly only when forced. It is the genesis volume of the Leatherstocking Tales.
lafontaine-fables-wright-1841:
Jean de La Fontaine published his Fables in France in books that appeared from 1668 onward. Elizur Wright turned them into English verse in 1841, and his version became a classic in its own right. The tales are short poems, most of them about animals who talk and scheme like people.

Foxes, wolves, ants, and grasshoppers act out pride, greed, folly, and wit. Each fable ends with a pointed moral, often sly rather than preachy. La Fontaine drew on Aesop and older sources but made the verse light, shrewd, and musical. French children still learn these poems by heart, and Wright's rhymes carry much of their charm into English.
stanhope-epictetus-simplicius-1741:
Epictetus, a freed slave who taught in Greece under the Roman Empire, left a short handbook of Stoic life called the Enchiridion. George Stanhope turned it into English, and his version first appeared in 1694. The fifth edition of 1741 adds the long commentary of Simplicius, a scholar of the sixth century, plus a life of Epictetus from Boileau.

Simplicius works through the handbook line by line, drawing out its rules on what we can and cannot control. For generations this was the form in which English readers met Stoic ethics. It stays the only pre-modern English version of Simplicius on the handbook.
al-masudi-meadows-of-gold-sprenger-1841:
Al-Masudi was a traveler from Baghdad. He saw India, Africa, and the Caspian lands in the tenth century, and he wrote the Muruj al-Dhahab, the Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems. Aloys Sprenger gave the first part of it English form in 1841. Only this first volume of his version ever appeared.

The Meadows is a cabinet of the world. It holds the making of the earth, the kings of Persia and India, the seas, the wonders, and the tales told in ports. Al-Masudi asks questions everywhere he goes and writes down what he hears, gold and dross together. Sprenger's volume lets English readers taste the great Arab Herodotus. The full French version stands in the library beside it.
miller-old-red-sandstone-1841:
Hugh Miller was a Scottish stonemason who taught himself geology in the quarries of Cromarty. His Old Red Sandstone, published in 1841, grew from letters written for a local paper. It made him famous almost at once.

Miller describes the strange fossil fishes locked in red rock layers near his home. He writes of their scales, fins, and armor with a poet's eye. At the time, such finds raised hard questions about the age of the earth. The book became a classic of popular geology for its clear prose and wonder. Stone by stone, he reads a vanished sea full of strange life.
fielding-shamela-1741:
Fielding's Shamela, from 1741, is the sharp little burlesque that started the novel wars. Its full title promises an apology for the life of Mrs Shamela Andrews. Fielding, writing under a comic mask, attacks Richardson's Pamela, the hit novel of the hour.

In letters like Richardson's own, Shamela lets readers see her true game: her virtue is bait to trap her master into marriage. The jokes expose the cant of the original while inventing a livelier rogue. Shamela runs to barely fifty pages, yet it launched Fielding toward Joseph Andrews. Readers still enjoy its wicked speed and its place in literary history.

plos-pone-0003741:

plos-pone-0003941:

fdr-day-of-infamy-1941:

atlantic-charter-1941:

No land hunger, the charter pledges, and self-rule for all peoples. Free trade, shared labor gains, and seas free to all follow. Victorious nations will disarm the beaten foes and guard the peace. massachusetts-body-of-liberties-1641:

Its clauses protect life, property, and fair trials, and they limit cruel punishments. Other parts cover women, children, servants, strangers, and even cruelty toward animals. Hong Sjölinder and Ann-Beth Jonsson published this infection imaging paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Meningococcal sepsis is a fast, often fatal blood infection. The authors use imaging to follow disease dynamics, how the infection develops and spreads in the body over time.

Sepsis kills by speed, so a clear picture of its timeline is clinically valuable. The approach turns a disease that unfolds in hidden stages into one that can be watched step by step. Watching the disease unfold in images shows which organs are hit and when. The work supports faster recognition and better-targeted treatment of meningococcal disease, where hours decide outcomes.
plos-pone-0000341:
Masaki Nishida and Matthew P. Walker published this sleep study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Daytime naps are known to help consolidate motor memory, locking in a practiced skill. The authors connect that benefit to sleep spindles, brief bursts of brain activity during sleep. They show the spindles act in regionally specific parts of the brain.

A nap is not uniform rest; specific rhythms in specific regions do the memory work. The study links spindle activity to the size of the learning gain after waking. The finding refines advice on naps and practice, and informs research on sleep-based rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0000441:
Carlos S. Moreno and colleagues tested a hard question about ovarian cancer treatment, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein p53, when working, can arrest the cell cycle, halting division. Chemotherapy often relies on cells dividing to kill them. The team gathered evidence that p53-mediated arrest can actually inhibit chemotherapeutic treatment of ovarian carcinomas.

The idea is uncomfortable: a protective protein might shelter tumor cells from the drugs meant to kill them, by putting them into a resting state. If so, a tumor's p53 status could predict whether a drug will help or underperform. The study warns that more cell-cycle arrest is not always better in cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0000541:
Kany-Kany Angelique Luabeya and colleagues ran a randomized controlled trial of supplements for South African children, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. The trial tested zinc or multiple micronutrient supplementation to reduce diarrhea and respiratory disease, two leading causes of child illness and death in poor regions.

Randomized trials are the gold standard because they separate the supplement's effect from luck and background differences. Zinc had strong prior evidence for diarrhea, while multi-micronutrient mixes were cheaper to deliver. A head-to-head trial in the children most affected tells programs which investment actually buys health.
plos-pone-0000641:
Shuxian Jiang, Yigong Fu, John Williams and colleagues described the cannabinoid system inside mouse embryonic stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. What decides whether a stem cell renews itself or becomes a specialized cell is a core question in biology. The team looked at two receptors, CB1 and CB2, and the cannabinoid signals that bind them.

They report where these receptors are expressed and what they do as stem cells form embryoid bodies and turn toward blood cell lines. Cannabinoids are best known from cannabis and from adult tissues. Finding their machinery at work in early embryos opens a new angle on how cell fate is steered.
plos-pone-0000741:
Mohammed Bakkali studied short bits of DNA that some bacteria go out of their way to take in. Many bacteria can absorb DNA from their surroundings and add it to their own genome. That uptake has real medical and money stakes, since it can spread drug resistance genes. Two bacterial families, Pasteurellaceae and Neisseriaceae, prefer DNA that carries certain short sequences.

Those favored sequences appear far more often in the bacteria's own genomes than chance would explain. Bakkali asks how such short sequences build up, move, and persist over time. One idea is self-recognition: by favoring their own sequence marks, bacteria trade genes mostly with kin. The study maps the pattern and weighs what could keep it in place.
plos-pone-0000841:
John P.A. Ioannidis, Nikolaos A. Patsopoulos and Evangelos Evangelou asked why pooled gene studies so often disagree with each other. A meta-analysis pools the results of many studies into one sum, and checks how much the parts differ. Such pooling was used more and more on genome-wide association studies. There, teams hunt the same gene effects and try to copy each other's finds.

The team's subject is heterogeneity: real gaps between study results. Some gaps are noise. Others are signs that groups, designs, or biases truly differ. Gene hunters who know how much gap to expect will not cheer too soon, or drop a true find too fast. The study is a guide to reading pooled claims with care.
plos-pone-0000941:
Biju Parekkadan, Daan van Poll, Kazuhiro Suganuma and colleagues tested whether molecules from stem cells can rescue a failing liver, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fulminant hepatic failure is sudden, severe liver collapse. Calming the immune system may offer a way out that avoids needing donor liver cells.

Mesenchymal stem cells, taken from bone marrow, are known to temper immune responses. The team asked whether the molecules these cells release, rather than the cells themselves, could reverse the failure. A cell free treatment would be easier to store, dose and approve. The study is an early step toward that idea, tested in a severe disease model.
plos-pone-0001041:
S. Hoyt Peckham, David Maldonado Diaz, Andreas Walli and colleagues documented turtle bycatch in small scale Pacific fisheries, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Industrial fishing bycatch, animals caught by accident, is known to harm seabirds, mammals and turtles. The impact of small scale coastal fisheries had been largely overlooked.

The team show that such fisheries jeopardize endangered Pacific loggerhead turtles. Small boats working close to shore can meet turtles where they feed and breed. Counting that harm changes the conservation ledger: protecting turtles means working with local fishers, not just fleets. The paper pairs the finding with the scale of coastal fishing worldwide.
plos-pone-0001141:
Northeast India is the only land bridge between the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. It may also have been a corridor for early human migrations into East Asia. B. Mohan Reddy and co-authors present genetic evidence on that route in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their focus is the Austro-Asiatic speaking tribes of the region.

The Austro-Asiatic language family is considered among the oldest in this part of Asia. The authors argue that these tribes supply a genetic link between South and Southeast Asia that had been missing. Their data bear on how the first peopling of East Asia unfolded.
plos-pone-0001241:
In some animals, RNA from mitochondria, the cell's power plants, turns up outside them, positioned in the egg at the spot that seeds germ cells. Youichirou Ninomiya and Shizuko Ichinose checked whether mammals do the same, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The phenomenon had been reported in several non-mammal groups but not in mammals.

The authors examined the expression and distribution of mitochondrial ribosomal RNA in the mouse oocyte and zygote. Whether the RNA localizes to a germ cell determinant in mammals bears on how universal that mechanism is. Their study brings the mammal case into an otherwise broader story.
plos-pone-0001341:
Two groups of tiny cyanobacteria, Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus, carry out much of the ocean's photosynthesis. Christophe Six and colleagues studied how they divide the ocean's light environment between them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Phytoplankton cells are entrained in the water column and so are often exposed to rapid changes in irradiance within the upper mixed layer.

The authors report that light variability illuminates niche-partitioning among marine picocyanobacteria: the groups specialize on different light regimes. Who wins where determines how much carbon the ocean fixes. Their work links a physical variable, flickering light, to global primary production.
plos-pone-0001441:
Farba Karam and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a blood test for hidden TB in people with HIV. Finding and treating hidden TB in this group can cut illness and death. The team tested a home built blood test that reads a key immune signal. They asked if the test stays sound as HIV gets worse.

They report the test kept its power to spot hidden TB in HIV patients. But its readings did shift with how far HIV had gone. That caveat matters for how results are read in clinics. The work supports use of the test, with care, in places where both ills are common.
plos-pone-0001541:
Phillipa Hay and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on eating disorder acts in South Australia. Proof on whether such ills are rising had been mixed. The team used two matched community surveys ten years apart. Both asked the same questions on eating acts in the general public.

They found that eating disorder acts had in fact risen over that span. A matched design makes the trend claim much firmer than loose reports. A real rise urges more funds for early care and school based guards. It also prompts work on what drove the rise in that decade.
plos-pone-0001641:
Arnaud Muller, Elise Glattard, Omar Taleb, and their co-authors measured morphine made by the body itself in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Morphine is best known as the main active drug in opium from poppies. Yet it also turns up in animal tissues and cell types, including the mammalian brain. Its making pathway had already been traced in a human nerve cell line.

The team studied a human cell line called SH-SY5Y and the cerebellum of mice to pin down where this in-house morphine occurs. The full text gives the detection methods and the amounts found. It also covers what the pattern suggests about why nerve cells would make a pain drug of their own. The work adds to the view that morphine-like signals form part of the brain's own chemistry, not just plant medicine.
plos-pone-0001741:
Vikram Paruchuri, Anil Prasad, Kevin McHugh, and their co-authors studied a calcium-binding protein in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. S100A7 is a small protein first noted in psoriatic skin lesions and later in squamous tumors of skin, lung, and breast. Its expression tracks with high-grade HER-positive tumors and a high risk of progression.

The team reports that lowering S100A7 inhibits signaling from epidermal growth factor in breast cancer cells. It also blocks the formation of osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. The full text gives the cell experiments and pathway readouts. Bone is where breast cancer often spreads, so a protein linking tumor signals to bone-eating cells is a target worth attention.
plos-pone-0001841:
Jordi Moya-Laraño, Dejan Vinković, Eva De Mas, and their co-authors modeled spider body evolution with pendulum physics in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Animals were thought to gain from pendulum mechanics as they hang and swing, trading height for speed. Convincing evidence was lacking.

The team shows the shape evolution of spiders is predicted by pendulum mechanics. Leg and body proportions match what good swinging needs. The full text gives the model and the species data. A law of physics that predicts anatomy across species is a rare result. It explains why hanging spiders evolved their marked long legged build.
plos-pone-0001941:
Nita Bharti and co-authors modeled how measles spreads along coasts in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Models help map how epidemics move through space and time, and what control steps might do. A leading model for spread between places, the gravity model, weighs both distance and the size of towns.

The team asked whether the mix of land and sea at coasts warps that spread in ways plain models miss. Coastal areas bunch people in lines and ports rather than even spreads. If models ignore that shape, they may misjudge where measles goes next. Better maps of spread help aim vaccines where they count most.
plos-pone-0002041:
Karine Bagramyan and co-authors built a test that spots botulinum toxin at vanishing levels, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Botulinum neurotoxin is among the most potent poisons known, a threat in spoiled food and a feared bioterror agent. A fast, cheap, and highly sensitive test for the active toxin in foods or blood was badly wanted.

As the title states, their method detects toxin type A at attomolar levels. That is a billionth of a billionth of a mole per liter, even in complex samples. Such sensitivity could flag tainted food early and let doctors track the toxin in patients.
plos-pone-0002141:
Amanda Dixon-McIver, Phil East, Charles Mein, and co-authors profiled small RNA molecules in leukemia patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Acute myeloid leukemia is the most common acute leukemia in adults, yet the gene changes behind it are still not fully mapped. The team measured 157 mature microRNAs, tiny RNAs that tune how genes are used.

Their samples came from 100 patients whose chromosome patterns, called karyotypes, covered the known range of the disease. Certain microRNA patterns matched certain karyotypes. Links like these can help sort patients into groups, which is a first step toward care and trials matched to each group's biology.
plos-pone-0002241:
Massimo Giuliani and co-authors grew a new kind of regulatory immune cell from blood stem cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural killer cells are known as killers of virus-infected and tumor cells. They can also regulate the immune system, but whether a defined NK subset does the regulating was in doubt.

The team used membrane-bound IL-15, a growth signal fixed to a surface, to guide blood CD34 progenitor cells into a novel regulatory NK subset. A lab source of calming immune cells could one day help control unwanted immune attacks, in transplantation or autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0002341:
Benjamin Elder and Kyriacos Athanasiou combined pressure and growth factors to grow tissues in the lab, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hydrostatic pressure is a real force in many tissues, including cartilage, the knee meniscus, the jaw joint disc, the spine's discs, bone, bladder. Blood vessels. Engineers growing replacement tissues need to know how pressure shapes growth.

The team tested hydrostatic pressure together with growth factors, the chemical signals that urge cells to build tissue. They found the two work together with synergistic and additive effects on tissue formation. Combining physical and chemical cues gives tissue engineers a stronger recipe for growing cartilage and like tissues.
plos-pone-0002441:

Their subject was retinoic acid promotes the generation of pancreatic endocrine progenitor cells and their further differentiation into β-Cells. plos-pone-0002941:
Ursula Mager, Tatjana Degenhardt, Leena Pulkkinen and co-authors checked ghrelin receptor gene variants in people with poor glucose tolerance in 2008. Ghrelin helps control appetite, energy balance, and body weight. Its effects run through the growth hormone secretagogue receptor, the GHSR gene product.

The team typed seven variants in that receptor gene and tested links to obesity and glucose handling. Participants already had impaired glucose tolerance, a step toward diabetes. Published in PLOS ONE, the study adds human data on a hunger hormone pathway often targeted in obesity drug research. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003041:
Zulfeqhar Syed, Torleif Härd, Anne Uv and co-authors surveyed mucin proteins in the fruit fly in 2008. In vertebrates, vital organs are shielded by barriers built largely from mucins. These proteins carry repeated stretches rich in proline and sugar-bearing amino acids, and their sequences are poorly conserved.

Whether fly mucins play comparable roles was the open question. A potential role for Drosophila mucins in development and physiology is the paper's claim, stated cautiously. Published in PLOS ONE, the fly offers a fast genetic model for mucus barrier biology tied to gut and lung health.
plos-pone-0003141:
Gerald Kastberger, Evelyn Schmelzer and Ilse Kranner study a striking defence by giant honeybees in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Apis dorsata nests in the open and has evolved many defence behaviours. Against wasps and hornets the bees show coordinated cascades like Mexican waves across the nest surface, a behaviour called shimmering. It starts at distinct spots on the nest.

The title states what the waves achieve: they repel hornets. Readers watch a colony act as one unit to drive off a predator without each bee having to fight. The study is a vivid case of group defence in social insects.
plos-pone-0003241:
Nicole C. Grieder and co-authors study a cell transport protein in the fruit fly in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. More and more work shows that tweaks to basic cell jobs shape how tissues form and how disease starts. The team made loss-of-function cases to learn what COPI coat transport does as the fly develops.

The title reports that one part, gammaCOP, is needed for protein release at the cell's top surface and for shaping epithelial sheets. Readers see a housekeeping job prove vital for building tissue. Flaws in basic transport can thus lie behind flaws in growth.
plos-pone-0003341:
Sandro Alves, Isabel Nascimento-Ferreira, Gwennaëlle Auregan and colleagues test RNA silencing for a brain disorder in rats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recent studies showed that RNA interference is a hopeful approach for treating autosomal dominant disorders. But wild-type and mutant transcripts must be told apart. The wild-type copy's expression and function must be preserved. A single nucleotide polymorphism is present in the target gene.

The title reports allele-specific RNA silencing of mutant ataxin-3 brings neuroprotection in a rat model of Machado-Joseph disease. Readers see gene therapy aimed at only the faulty copy. That precision is the key hurdle for dominant inherited brain diseases.
plos-pone-0007441: When the environment shifts, bacteria reorganize their chemistry — and this systems-level study asked which of E. coli's metabolic relationships stay steady through the change. The researchers measured how levels of small molecules move together under different stresses. Finding both stable and shifting links gives a map of which parts of the cell's economy are rigid and which adapt.
plos-pone-0007541: ERK1 is a well-known signal carrier usually found in the cell's main compartment, but this study caught it associating with mitochondria in human cells. The unexpected location suggests the MAPK pathway has business at the cell's power plants. The finding opens a new chapter on where and how this famous signal operates.
plos-pone-0007641: Before birth, the fetal liver doubles as a blood factory, then hands the job to bone marrow. This study tracked gene and protein activity through the mid-pregnancy liver to watch the handover between blood-making and liver-building. The dynamic profiles capture an organ mid-career-change.
plos-pone-0007741: When a livestock virus spreads, math can guide the response. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Szmaragd and colleagues built a modeling framework for bluetongue virus transmission within and between farms in Great Britain. Unlike earlier livestock models built for direct-contact spread, this one handles a midge-borne virus. Policymakers can use it to test control measures before outbreaks force costly guesses.
plos-pone-0007841: Two major cell-signaling highways were found to intersect. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Crampton and colleagues showed the beta-catenin-dependent Wnt pathway links to integrin signaling through the adaptor protein Grb2. Wnt signals branch from frizzled receptors while integrins sense the cell's surroundings. Finding their junction explains how growth and matrix cues combine to steer cell behavior.
plos-pone-0007941: The Lyme-disease spirochete's plasmids are restless, full of jumping genes. This study found stem-loop sequences from the IS605 transposon linked to lipoprotein genes on Borrelia plasmids. The association hints at how the pathogen shuffles its surface disguise.
plos-pone-0008041: Bloodstream infections got a same-day ID method. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by La Scola and Raoult identified bacteria directly from positive blood culture bottles using MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry. Slow cultures blunt emergency care. The rapid fingerprinting could get patients the right antibiotics hours sooner.
plos-pone-0008141: After spinal cord injury, a glial scar blocks regrowth — but it also calls for help. This rat study found scar astrocytes attract migrating olfactory ensheathing cells via secreted TNF-α. The scar's signal could be harnessed for repair.
plos-pone-0008241: Milk's sugar coating got a fresh look. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Duncan's team revisited sialic acid use and synthesis in newborn rats. The sugar decorates milk and many newborn molecules; the brain is especially hungry for it. Tracing its fate tests whether milk evolved to feed the growing brain. The revisit updates a classic nutrition story.
plos-pone-0008341: Childhood TB got a faster test. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Ha's team tried the MODS drug-susceptibility assay for early TB diagnosis in Vietnamese children. The liquid-culture method watches germs grow under the microscope. Among 217 samples, it beat slow standard cultures. The speed matters where childhood TB hides.
plos-pone-0008441: Diseased proteins' tipping points were mapped. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Liu and Zhao modeled the switch region where pathogenic protein misfolding begins. Destabilized patches flip first. The team also predicted the regions from sequence. The tipping-point map aids misfolding-disease research.
plos-pone-0008541: Diabetes genes were weighed against body fat. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Pecioska's team tested whether type 2 diabetes loci track measures of fatness. Most patients are obese; the arrow of causality was murky. The locus-fatness links were mapped. The results disentangle genes, fat, and diabetes.
plos-pone-0008641: A brain-region marker got discovered. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Uhde's team identified Rmst, a non-coding RNA marking the mouse ventral mesencephalic floor plate. The developing brain needed better labels. The marker's pattern was mapped. The label aids developmental neuroscience.
plos-pone-0008741: Stimulants' signal boost got a brain locus. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Shin's team showed amphetamine in the ventral striatum facilitates responses to visual reward cues in rats. The incentive-boost circuit was mapped. The locus informs addiction science.
plos-pone-0008841: Canary food rebels got a watch. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Cadieu's team watched canaries try new foods and copy each other. The rebel-copy dance was mapped in the flock. The watch feeds animal-culture science.
plos-pone-0008941: Pregnancy's immune peace got a dock map. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Gonen-Gross's team mapped how womb-side docks read the HLA-G peace flag. The touch-point rules were mapped. The map feeds baby-immune science.
plos-pone-0009041: A malaria shot got a Mali kid trial. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Thera's team tested the AMA1 malaria vaccine FMP2.1/AS02A for safety and immunogenicity in Malian children. The phase 1 dose escalation was run. The trial advances malaria vaccines.
plos-pone-0009141: Fly stress circuits got a neuron map. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Zhao's team showed corazonin neurons wire sexually dimorphic stress-response circuits in Drosophila. The behavioral circuitry was mapped. The map informs stress neurobiology.
plos-pone-0009241: Chimpanzee culture was linked to female group size. This 2010 PLOS ONE study by Lind and Lindenfors found that the number of cultural traits in chimpanzee communities correlates with female group size but not male group size. While human models tie cultural complexity to population size, the chimpanzee pattern points to females as culture's carriers. The finding reframes how traditions spread and persist in our closest relatives.
plos-pone-0009341: The eye's back wall got a gene hunt plan. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Booij's team planned a gene hunt for the eye's back wall. The hunt plan was checked. The plan feeds sight-loss research.
plos-pone-0011441: Metallothioneins are small proteins that soak up toxic metals, and measuring them at trace levels matters for environmental and medical testing. This research paper presents an electrochemical method sensitive enough to detect them at the zeptomole scale — a vanishingly small amount. The ultra-sensitive technique gives labs a new tool for catching metal-binding proteins where older methods saw nothing.
plos-pone-0011541: MicroRNAs fine-tune development, and pigs are a key model for human biology. This research paper catalogs the microRNAome — the full set of microRNAs — across pig development before and after birth. The developmental atlas gives researchers a baseline for studying how these tiny regulators shape growth.
plos-pone-0011641: Antibodies improve through deliberate DNA mutation by the enzyme AID — and histones mark the spots. This research paper finds histones H2A and H2B get single ubiquitin tags at AID-targeted loci. The histone flags reveal how the cell aims its mutating machinery at antibody genes.
plos-pone-0011741: A strep germ called dysgalactiae equisimilis causes sore throats and sometimes invades the bloodstream. plos-pone-0011941: VEGF-C drives vessel growth — and blocking it fights disease. This research paper builds phage-derived human antibody fragments against VEGF-C that block its VEGF receptor-2 and 3 binding. The blockers offer a therapeutic grip on runaway vessel growth in the body.
